name: Phosphorus
kicker: Element 15 · The glowing element in matches, bones, and DNA
briefing: In 1669, the German alchemist Hennig Brand boiled down huge amounts of urine, hoping to find the secret of making gold, and instead got a waxy substance that glowed in the dark. He had found phosphorus, whose name means “light-bearer” in Greek. Its red form coats the striking strip on a matchbox, and phosphate groups containing it hold together your DNA and help ATP power your cells.
answerHtml: Phosphorus (accept P; accept white phosphorus or red phosphorus; do not accept “phosphate”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Joseph Wright of Derby painted an alchemist kneeling beside a glowing flask as he discovers this element. In real life, Hennig Brand first made it in 1669 by boiling down large amounts of urine while searching for the philosopher’s stone.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, whose red form is used on the strips for striking matches.

tossups.p: Despite this element’s name, the faint green glow of its white form is not phosphorescence but chemiluminescence, caused by a slow reaction with oxygen in the air. That white form can burst into flame on its own, so it is stored under water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, found in the phosphate groups of DNA.

tossups.p: The 1906 Berne Convention banned this element’s white form from matches, because factory workers who handled it could develop a bone disease of the jaw nicknamed “phossy jaw.” Strike-anywhere match heads later used a safer compound of this element and sulfur instead.
tossups.r: Safety matches use its red form on the striking strip. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase labeled viral DNA with a radioactive isotope of this element and viral protein with radioactive sulfur, helping show that DNA is the genetic material. Hennig Brand had first isolated this element from urine in 1669.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element found in the phosphate groups of DNA and ATP, number 15 on the periodic table.

tossups.p: Antoine Lavoisier [“lah-vwah-zee-AY”] showed that this element and sulfur gain mass when they burn, because they combine with part of the air, helping overthrow the phlogiston theory. Burning this element makes a white smoke of its oxide, which soaks up water so strongly that chemists use it as a drying agent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, whose red form is used on the striking strips of matchboxes.

tossups.p: This element shares its name with the ancient Greek name for the planet Venus seen as the morning star, since both names mean “light-bearer.” This element’s white form glows faintly in the dark as it slowly reacts with oxygen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, number 15 on the periodic table, used in matches and fertilizers.

tossups.p: In 1842, John Bennet Lawes patented a fertilizer called superphosphate, made by treating rock rich in this element with sulfuric acid. Seabird droppings called guano, dug from islands off Peru, were another important early source of this plant nutrient.
tossups.r: Fertilizers supply it along with nitrogen and potassium. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: Unlike the carbon and nitrogen cycles, the cycle of this element has no major stage as a gas in the atmosphere, so it moves mainly through rocks, soil, water, and living things. Weathering rocks slowly release this element as ions that plants absorb through their roots.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a key nutrient in fertilizer along with nitrogen and potassium.

tossups.p: Many U.S. states limited this element’s compounds in laundry and dishwasher detergents, because wastewater carrying them fed huge algal blooms in lakes, a process called eutrophication [“yoo-troh-fih-KAY-shun”]. Runoff from fertilized farm fields carries this element into rivers and lakes too.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15, which fertilizers supply along with nitrogen and potassium.

tossups.p: Black, the most stable form of this element, has stacked, puckered layers like graphite, and sheets one atom thick can be peeled off it much like graphene. Heating this element’s white form without air turns it into a red form that is far less dangerous to handle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, number 15, whose red form coats the strips used to strike safety matches.

tossups.p: About a century after this element was first found, Johan Gahn and Carl Wilhelm Scheele [“SHAY-luh”] learned to make it from bone ash, a far richer source than urine. Bones and teeth get their hardness from a calcium mineral called hydroxyapatite [“hy-DROK-see-AP-uh-tite”], which contains this element.
tossups.r: Phosphate groups containing it link the sugars in DNA. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: Cell membranes are built from two layers of molecules whose water-loving heads contain this element and whose tails are fatty acids. Inside cells, enzymes called kinases switch many proteins on or off by attaching groups containing this element to them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element found in ATP and in the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA.

tossups.p: Morocco holds most of the world’s known reserves of a rock that is mined for this element, and large deposits are also mined in Florida. Many plants team up with root fungi called mycorrhizae [“my-koh-RYE-zee”] to help gather this nutrient from the soil.
tossups.r: Fertilizer labels list its amount second, after nitrogen and before potassium. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: Each molecule of this element’s white form has four atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron, and the strain in their tightly bent bonds makes that form very reactive. That white form must be kept under water, because it can catch fire on its own in air.
tossups.r: Its safer red form is used on the strips for striking matches. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 15.

tossups.p: An acid containing this element gives cola drinks their tangy taste and is used in rust removers that turn rust into a protective coating. Many insecticides, such as malathion [“MAL-uh-thy-on”], are organic compounds of this element.
tossups.r: Its phosphate groups are in ATP and DNA. For 10 points, name this element, whose red form is used to strike matches.

trap.title: Element, not phosphate
trap.body: Many clues about DNA, ATP, bones, and fertilizer mention “phosphate,” a group made of this element bonded to oxygen, so players blurt “phosphate” when the question wants the element. “Phosphor” and “phosphorescence” are traps too: despite the name, white phosphorus glows because of a slow reaction with oxygen (chemiluminescence), not phosphorescence.
trap.fix: If the question says “this element” or gives the atomic number 15, say phosphorus. Phosphate is the answer only for “this ion” or “this group.” Nitrogen, directly above it, is element 7 and makes up 78 percent of the air.
trap.line: Real answer line: Phosphorus (accept P; accept white phosphorus or red phosphorus; do not accept “phosphate”)
